conceptTag: Set goals for a product team
readerTitle: Eleven goals, five people: planning a product team's quarter
caseNote: 가상 사례 (유통 체인의 자체 브랜드 상품팀, 사무용 의자 제조사 상품팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 상품팀의 목표는 '무엇을 만들까'가 아니라 '고객에게 무엇이 달라질까'를 적고, 그 목표를 지키려고 무엇을 하지 않을지까지 정하는 일이다.
misconception: 출시 개수처럼 할 일을 목표로 적고, 중요한 일은 전부 목록에 넣어 두면 팀이 더 많이 해낸다.

sources.text: Doerr, J. (2018). Measure What Matters. Portfolio (OKR의 목표·핵심 결과 구분)
Grove, A. (1983). High Output Management. Random House

factChecks.note: 모든 수치(재구매율 18%→25%, 반품률 6%→3%, 팀 5명, 목표 11개)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다.
이 레슨은 적용 레슨으로 새 개념을 소개하지 않습니다. 사용 개념: OKR(OPS-04-02), 너무 많이 하는 비용(OPS-04-05). 형제 레슨 OPS-04-07(카페)과 상황이 겹치지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Eleven goals, five people
body: Maya runs the own-label team at a regional grocery chain. Her five people create the store's own brand of snacks, sauces and cleaning products.
It's the first Monday of the quarter. The whiteboard already holds eleven goals, each one added by someone with a good reason. By Friday, Maya has to turn that board into a plan.

image.label: A crowded whiteboard with eleven sticky-note goals
image.brief: 사무실 화이트보드에 포스트잇 11장이 빽빽하게 붙어 있고, 그 앞에 팀원 5명이 서 있는 장면. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트. 포스트잇에는 "New chips", "Fix labels", "Cut costs" 같은 짧은 문구. 실제 유통사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which goal would you write at the top?
body: Store-brand snacks sell well when they're new, then fade. Leadership wants the range to earn its shelf space.
Which line belongs at the top of Maya's plan?

options.text: Launch 12 new own-label snacks this quarter
options.feedback: Clear and easy to track, but it measures activity, not results. In **objectives and key results**, a key result shows what changed for customers. The team could hit 12 launches while nobody buys a second bag.

options.text: Make our snacks a reason to come back: repeat buyers rise from 18% to 25%
options.feedback: This is an **objective and key result**: a direction people care about, plus a number that proves it happened. It leaves the team free to choose how, whether that's new flavors, better packs or fewer weak products.
The direction is right, but with no number or deadline, nobody can tell in week 10 whether they're on track. A good objective needs a measurable key result beside it.

cards.title: From a to-do list to a result
body: Maya rewrites the top of the board. **Objective:** customers come back for our snacks. **Key results:** repeat buyers from 18% to 25%, and two of the five slowest sellers replaced.
The launches don't disappear. They become one possible way to move the numbers. If a better recipe for an existing chip does more than three new ones, the plan allows it.
cards.softwareNote: In a software product team, "ship 10 features" is the launch count. A key result looks like "share of new users who finish setup in week one rises from 40% to 55%."

cards.title: Now, what about the other ten goals?
body: Every item on the board has a sponsor: cleaner labels, a cheaper sauce supplier, a holiday range, a new pack size and more.
What should Maya do with them?

options.text: Keep all eleven, but rank them so people know what comes first
options.feedback: Ranking helps, but a list of eleven still invites everyone to start everything. This is **the cost of doing too much**: work gets spread thin and little finishes.

options.text: Keep two or three objectives and write a visible "not this quarter" list
options.feedback: The team gets real time on what matters, and the parked ideas aren't lost. Saying no in writing is how you avoid **the cost of doing too much**.

options.text: Give each of the five people two goals to own
options.feedback: Everyone feels responsible, but each goal gets one part-time person and nobody can help a colleague. It hides **the cost of doing too much** instead of cutting it.

cards.title: Same team, very different focus
body: Five people for a 12-week quarter is about 60 person-weeks of work. Fewer goals means each one gets enough time to actually finish.

breakdown.label: Per goal, with 11 goals
breakdown.detail: Barely a person for a month each

breakdown.label: Per goal, with 3 goals
breakdown.detail: Almost two people for the full quarter

cards.callout: And that's before switching between tasks eats into the time.

cards.title: A good number can still be gamed.
body: Repeat buyers could jump to 25% with a deep discount, and the team would "win" while losing money. Add a guardrail to the key result, such as: snack margin stays where it is.
Also, a short goal list doesn't erase routine work. Labels still need fixing when a law or recipe changes. Count that work first, then set goals with the time that's left.

cards.title: Now it's a chair factory.
body: You lead the product team at a company that makes office chairs. About 6 in 100 chairs come back, mostly for wobbly armrests. Your team also has four new models in the works.
Which plan for next quarter is strongest?

options.text: Objective: fewer chairs come back. Key result: returns from 6% to 3%. Pause two of the new models.
options.feedback: A result customers feel, a number to check it, and the time freed to reach it. It uses both **objectives and key results** and the discipline of doing less.

options.text: Ship all four new models, redesign the armrest and cut returns
options.feedback: Three big goals for one team. Everything moves a little and the armrest fix, the one hurting customers now, competes for time. That's **the cost of doing too much**.

options.text: Hold a weekly quality meeting on returns
options.feedback: A useful habit, but it's an activity, not a result. Meetings can happen every week while returns stay at 6%. Pair it with a key result.

cards.softwareNote: A software team faces the same pull: a bug that drives users away versus a roadmap full of new features. The fix usually wins the quarter.

cards.title: Write the result you want, then protect the time to get it.
body: Two ideas from this unit did the work today:
list: **Objectives and key results:** state what changes for customers and the number that proves it, not a count of launches
**The cost of doing too much:** fewer goals and a written "not this quarter" list give each goal enough time to finish
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take your team's goal list. Rewrite one activity as a result with a number, and move one goal to "not this quarter."
